records.sourceFile: What Does Mental Rest Mean to Professional Athletes - A Study of National Football League Players.pdf

paper.citation: Eccles DW, Twedell H, DeCouto BS. What does mental rest mean to professional athletes? A study of National Football League players. Psychology of Sport & Exercise. 2026;82:103029.
paper.abstract: Sixteen NFL players were interviewed about mental rest, and a thematic analysis tested whether an existing model of mental rest from college athletes applies to professional athletes. The model generalized well, with sleep and several wakeful resting experiences found, but public recognition and job pressures created departures from the model. Mental rest was linked by players to concentration, recovery and health.
paper.tldr: NFL players described mental rest in ways that largely match a model built on college athletes, including a break from thinking about football and a sense of control over one's time. Public recognition and job insecurity made it harder for them to switch off, so rest planning should account for these pressures.
paper.methods: Qualitative description design with semi-structured interviews of 16 NFL players recruited through personal contacts and one franchise's clinical psychologist. Interviews lasted 13 to 45 minutes. A medium-Q thematic analysis was conducted by one researcher, with a critical friend, using codes from the Eccles-Kazmier model plus inductive codes.
paper.findings: Players described sleep and wakeful resting, and six of the seven wakeful resting experiences in the model were found, including a break from thinking about sport and from effortful thinking, control over one's life, and a break from routines and training demands. Constant thinking about football was linked to job precarity and family income pressure. Players reported that public recognition often blocked escape, so they stayed home or avoided public places. The academic work experience in the model was not found.
paper.limitations: Each player was interviewed once in a short session, and the sample was convenience-based and mostly African American, which differs from the college sample in the model. The findings describe experiences and do not estimate how common they are, and they may not extend to less recognizable professional athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest helping players choose in-season rest activities that give several breaks at once (from football, from effortful thinking, from routine) and fitting them into the easiest points of a busy week. For recognizable players, consider identifying rest locations with few football cues, since players reported that public places often brought unwanted football conversations.
paper.athleteDev: Players linked poor mental rest to weaker concentration, more mental errors and lower physical output in their own words. Use this to support in-season routines that include low-demand, non-football activities and time with family, and plan rest locations with few football cues.
paper.rtp: Limited use. The study examined mental rest in active NFL players and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or set criteria for them.

records.sourceFile: Spatiotemporal kinematics during top speed sprinting in male intercollegiate track and field and team sport athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Meng CR, Walts CT, Ryan LJ, Stearne DJ, Clark KP. Spatiotemporal kinematics during top speed sprinting in male intercollegiate track and field and team sport athletes. Sports Biomechanics. 2024.
paper.abstract: Ninety-eight male intercollegiate track and field and team sport athletes completed 40 m sprints filmed for analysis between 30 and 40 m. Contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor were meaningfully correlated with top speed. At matched top speeds, team sport athletes used a more ground-based pattern, with longer contact times and shorter flight times, than slower track athletes, so track-based technical models may need modification for team sport athletes.
paper.tldr: Across 98 male college athletes, the sprint measures that tracked top speed were contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor. Team sport athletes reached the same top speed as slower track athletes but with more ground contact, so track-based sprint models may not fit team sport athletes directly.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study with 98 male varsity athletes (28 track and field, 70 team sport) tested in one session. Two 40 m sprints per athlete were filmed at 240 frames per second, and the faster 30 to 40 m split was analysed with Kinovea using five-frame stride digitizing. Pearson or Spearman correlations were used across the sample, and independent t tests compared matched slow track (n = 14) and fast team sport (n = 22) subgroups with a Bonferroni-adjusted alpha of 0.007.
paper.findings: Across all athletes, contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor were meaningfully correlated with top speed (0.51 to 0.78), and flight time and contact length were weakly correlated (0.27 to 0.34). In matched subgroups at about 9.3 m/s, team sport athletes had longer contact time (0.114 vs 0.104 s), shorter flight time (0.109 vs 0.124 s), longer contact length (1.06 vs 0.97 m), shorter flight length (1.02 vs 1.16 m) and higher duty factor (0.255 vs 0.228), while step rate and step length did not differ significantly.
paper.limitations: Only male athletes were studied, track athletes ran in sneakers rather than spikes, and the analysis used a single sagittal video view, one stride, one rater (intra-rater differences of about 0.2% to 1.6%) and a 30 to 40 m field of view. The subgroup comparison used small samples, and Fast team sport athletes were about 7 kg heavier than Slow track athletes. Force, energy cost and joint angles were not measured, so the paper cannot show whether the team sport pattern is more efficient or safer.
paper.practicalImplications: Use contact time, step rate, step length, flight length and duty factor as descriptive measures of top speed sprinting, but do not assume that a track-style pattern is the target for team sport athletes. Team sport athletes who reach the same top speed may do so with longer ground contact and a higher duty factor, so coaches should be cautious about applying track-based technical models and normative metrics to them.
paper.athleteDev: Profile sprint mechanics in team sport athletes without assuming a track-only reference. Faster team sport athletes here reached similar top speed with longer contact time and a higher duty factor, but the authors also note that training toward a track model might raise top speed, so neither pattern was shown to be the better target.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. Athletes were injury-free and the study did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Acute Changes in Hamstring Injury Risk Factors After a Session of High-Volume Maximal Sprinting Speed Efforts in Soccer Players.pdf

paper.citation: Carmona G, Moreno-Simonet L, Cosio PL, Astrella A, Fernández D, Padullés X, et al. Acute changes in hamstring injury risk factors after a session of high-volume maximal sprinting speed efforts in soccer players. Sports Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: Fifteen healthy male amateur soccer players completed 10 maximal 40 m sprints, and sprint performance, posterior chain strength, range of motion, dynamic pelvic tilt and muscle damage markers were measured for 72 hours afterward. Top speed and posterior chain strength declined for 48 to 72 hours and creatine kinase and soreness rose, while the pelvic tilt change was not significant. The authors suggest that sprint dosage could be individualized by risk factor profile, which was not tested.
paper.tldr: In healthy amateur soccer players, a session of 10 maximal 40 m sprints reduced top speed and posterior chain strength for 48 to 72 hours and raised muscle damage markers. Individual responses varied widely, so sprint planning should consider recovery time and individual monitoring.
paper.methods: Prospective observational case series with a single group of 15 healthy male amateur soccer players. Players performed 10 maximal 40 m sprints with 3 minutes of rest. Measures at baseline and 24, 48 and 72 hours included 10 m and 30 m sprint times, theoretical maximal force and velocity from a field force-velocity method, 90:20 isometric posterior chain strength, hip flexor and hamstring range of motion, dynamic pelvic tilt from an inertial sensor, serum creatine kinase and perceived soreness. Analysis used bootstrap effect sizes against baseline.
paper.findings: Theoretical maximal velocity was reduced through 48 hours (9.05 to 8.65 m/s, ES -0.71), and 30 m time was slower at 48 and 72 hours. Posterior chain strength was reduced through 48 hours in the non-dominant leg (192 to 166 N, ES -0.60) and through 72 hours in the dominant leg (213 to 194 N, ES -0.40). Creatine kinase peaked at 24 hours (840 U/L, ES 1.28) and soreness peaked at 48 hours. Dynamic pelvic tilt rose non-significantly (P = 0.06), and range of motion showed no significant change.
paper.limitations: The study had one group, no control condition and only 15 players, and the authors describe it as a pilot. Individual responses varied widely, so group means may hide player-level patterns, and the study did not include lower-limb kinematics, injury outcomes or players by position. The Discussion gives a different Sdec value (3.62%) from the Results (3.67%).
paper.practicalImplications: After a high-volume maximal sprint session like this one, expect top speed and posterior chain strength to stay reduced for up to 48 to 72 hours in amateur players; some deficits were still present at 72 hours, the last time point measured. Check individual responses before scheduling further maximal sprint volume, since responses varied widely; the authors suggest but did not test individualizing sprint dosage by risk factor profile.
paper.athleteDev: Use this to inform sprint dosage in healthy amateur players: a single session of 10 maximal 40 m sprints reduced top speed and strength for 48 to 72 hours. The study did not test when the next high-speed exposure is safe, and responses varied widely, so monitor individuals rather than applying the group average.
paper.rtp: Limited. The players were healthy and no injured players were tested, so the findings describe recovery after sprinting in healthy players and cannot set return-to-play criteria or show when strength or sprint capacity is safe after a hamstring injury.

records.sourceFile: Reliability and Sensitivity of Nocturnal Heart Rate and Heart-Rate Variability in Monitoring Individual Responses to Training Load.pdf

paper.citation: Nuuttila O-P, Seipäjärvi S, Kyröläinen H, Nummela A. Reliability and sensitivity of nocturnal heart rate and heart-rate variability in monitoring individual responses to training load. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022. (Ahead of print.)
paper.abstract: Recreational runners recorded nocturnal heart rate and heart rate variability after two identical low-intensity sessions (n = 15) and before and after a 3000 m test (n = 23). Night-to-night reliability was very high for all indices and segments. After the 3000 m test, heart rate rose and heart rate variability fell in the 4-hour and full-night segments, but not in the morning value.
paper.tldr: Wearable nocturnal heart rate and HRV were highly reliable from night to night in recreational runners. After a hard 3000 m test, the 4-hour and full-night values showed clear changes, but the morning value did not.
paper.methods: Recreational male and female runners wore a Firstbeat Bodyguard 2 device overnight. Average heart rate, LnRMSSD and LnHF were calculated for a full night, a 4-hour segment starting 30 minutes after sleep onset, and a morning value. Reliability was tested with ICC and CV after two identical low-intensity sessions (n = 15); sensitivity was tested with repeated-measures models after a rest day versus the night after a 3000 m test (n = 23).
paper.findings: After the two low-intensity sessions, nights were similar, with ICC of 0.97 to 0.98 for heart rate, 0.92 to 0.97 for LnRMSSD and 0.91 to 0.96 for LnHF, and between-night CV of 2.1% to 3.8%. After the 3000 m test, the 4-hour segment showed heart rate rising from 51.2 to 55.0 bpm and LnRMSSD falling from 4.19 to 4.02 ms. The full-night segment showed similar changes, while the morning value did not change.
paper.limitations: The reliability sample (n = 15) and sensitivity sample (n = 23) were small, and many possible participants were excluded for lack of full-night data. Sexes were not analyzed separately, and readiness to train was the only external reference for recovery. Bedtime was later after the 3000 m test, which may have affected the nocturnal values.
paper.practicalImplications: Nocturnal recordings can be used for resting heart rate and HRV monitoring in recreational runners, because the day-to-day variation is low. Use the same segment consistently; after a hard test, the 4-hour and full-night values showed clear changes while the morning value did not, so the choice of segment affects the interpretation.
paper.athleteDev: Use nocturnal heart rate and HRV in endurance athletes to track responses to hard sessions, and keep one analysis segment for each athlete. The sensitivity results come from recreational runners, so confirm the response to maximal efforts in the athletes being monitored.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study used recreational runners without injury and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Reliability and validity of the end range hamstring strength test with handheld dynamometry.pdf

paper.citation: Kristiansen J, Eddy C, Magnusson SP. Reliability and validity of the end range hamstring strength test with handheld dynamometry. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;19(3):268-274.
paper.abstract: Twenty healthy active participants were tested for hamstring strength in a lengthened position with a handheld dynamometer and an isokinetic Biodex on two days. Handheld dynamometer scores correlated strongly with the Biodex, and intra-rater reliability was excellent while inter-rater reliability was moderate to good. The authors conclude that the test is a reliable and valid, low-cost option for measuring hamstring strength at long muscle lengths.
paper.tldr: A handheld dynamometer test of hamstring strength in a lengthened position agreed well with an isokinetic machine and was reliable when the same tester repeated it. Inter-rater reliability was weaker, especially for the left leg.
paper.methods: Twenty healthy active participants were tested with the Biodex and a handheld dynamometer on test day 1, and the handheld test was repeated 7 to 10 days later by two testers. Pearson correlations, Bland-Altman plots, paired t tests and ICC (two-way random, single measure, consistency) with SEM and minimal detectable difference were calculated.
paper.findings: Handheld dynamometer and Biodex scores correlated strongly (r = 0.87 right, r = 0.911 left), and Bland-Altman mean differences were 12 N (left) and 22 N (right) with all points inside the limits of agreement. There was no systematic bias between test days or testers. Intra-rater ICC was 0.91 right and 0.93 left (SEM 8.5% and 8.2%, minimal detectable differences 26.3% and 24.2%), and inter-rater ICC was 0.83 right and 0.71 left (SEM 11.2% and 16.1%, minimal detectable differences 34.9% and 47.7%).
paper.limitations: The sample was 20 healthy active participants recruited by convenience, including hospital employees and local club athletes, and sex was not reported in the text. Two testers of different sex, handedness and experience were used, the left-leg inter-rater ICC had a wide 95% CI (0.39 to 0.87), the first test day was not blinded, and Bland-Altman plots suggested larger differences at higher force. The abstract gives r = 0.87 for both legs and the Discussion gives SEM ranges that differ from Table 2; the Results and Table 2 values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the handheld dynamometer end-range hamstring test with the same tester for repeat measures. Only changes larger than about 24% to 26% for same-tester testing, and much larger changes between testers, should be treated as real. The test has not been validated for injured athletes, so it cannot set return-to-play thresholds.
paper.athleteDev: Use this low-cost test to profile hamstring strength at long muscle lengths in athletes, with the same tester for repeat tests. Do not read small changes as real because the measurement error is large.
paper.rtp: Limited use. The authors suggest the test may help monitor rehabilitation and detect deficits before and after return to play, but the sample was healthy participants, so it does not establish injury-specific cutoffs or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: The test-retest reliability of force plate-derived parameters of the countermovement push-up as a power assessment tool.pdf

paper.citation: Parry GN, Herrington LC, Horsley IG. The test-retest reliability of force plate-derived parameters of the countermovement push-up as a power assessment tool. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(3):381-383.
paper.abstract: This test-retest study measured force plate variables from the countermovement push-up in 10 male college athletes on two occasions 7 days apart. No differences were found between sessions. Intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.88 to 0.98 across parameters, with peak force and mean force reliable and rate of force development the least reliable.
paper.tldr: Peak force, mean force, flight time and impulse from a force plate countermovement push-up were reliable across two sessions in 10 male college athletes, while rate of force development was not. Whether the test detects training change was not studied.
paper.methods: Single-group repeated-measures test-retest design. Ten male college athletes, each performing three maximal-effort countermovement push-ups on two force plates on two occasions 7 days apart. Flight time, peak force, mean force, rate of force development and impulse were taken from the force-time curve and analyzed with paired t tests, ICC, CV, SEM and SDD.
paper.findings: No significant differences were found between the two test occasions for any measure (P greater than .05). Flight time, peak force, mean force and impulse had ICC of 0.96 to 0.98 and CV of 1.7% to 6.9%, while rate of force development fell outside acceptable reliability (CV 14.1%, ICC 0.878). The smallest detectable differences were 7.5% for peak force, 8.6% for mean force and 11.2% for rate of force development, and impulse had an SDD of 26.1% in Table 1.
paper.limitations: The sample was 10 male college athletes, so estimates are imprecise and may not apply to other groups, and responsiveness to training was not tested. The abstract reports CV of 5.5% to 14.1% while Table 1 shows 1.7% to 14.1%, the Discussion gives the RFD CV as 14.9%, and some Table 1 values do not reconcile with the stated formulas (mean force SEM 1.7 N with SDD 50.3 N); the Results and Table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: In similar trained college athletes, peak force and mean force from the countermovement push-up can be tracked, treating only changes larger than about 7.5% for peak force and 8.6% for mean force as beyond measurement error (the authors suggest 8% to 9%). Avoid relying on rate of force development, and expect impulse to need a change of about 26% before it exceeds measurement error.
paper.athleteDev: Use peak and mean force from the force plate countermovement push-up to monitor upper-body power in similar college athletes, using the reported smallest detectable differences to judge real change. Do not use rate of force development as a tracking measure until its reliability is shown.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study tested reliability in active college athletes and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport readiness, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries- a systematic review, qualitative analysis and metaanalysis.pdf

paper.citation: Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med 2018;0:1-8.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled six randomised controlled trials of strength training for sports injury prevention in 7738 participants aged 12-40 years. The cluster-adjusted intention-to-treat relative risk was 0.338 (95% CI 0.238 to 0.480), and the authors report a dose-dependent relationship between strength training volume and intensity and injury reduction.
paper.tldr: Across six randomised trials, mostly in soccer players, strength training reduced sports injuries by about two-thirds overall. Larger weekly training volume and higher intensity were associated with bigger reductions.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42015006970) of randomised trials of strength training for primary sports injury prevention, searched to July 2017. Two reviewers screened studies and rated risk of bias, and the authors pooled cluster-adjusted relative risks, rated GRADE certainty, tested heterogeneity and publication bias, and ran a post hoc meta-regression of volume, intensity and duration.
paper.findings: Six trials (7738 participants, 177 injuries) gave a pooled relative risk of 0.338 with no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), rated high certainty by GRADE, and no publication bias was detected. In the post hoc meta-regression, a 10% increase in weekly repetitions was associated with the pooled relative risk falling from 0.338 to 0.295 (4.3 percentage points, 13% relative), and higher intensity was also associated with lower risk, while duration was not significant. Four trials reported no adverse events among 3991 participants.
paper.limitations: Trial populations, programmes and injury definitions differed, and one trial was excluded from the meta-regression for insufficient data. The dose-response result comes from a post hoc analysis across trials, so it does not show that individuals who train at a higher dose will be protected to the same degree. Compliance was high in research settings, and the authors note club adherence remains a challenge.
paper.practicalImplications: Strength training programmes with adequate weekly volume and intensity can be used for sports injury prevention, with a familiarisation or technique phase before progressive loading, as the authors recommend. The review does not show equal benefit in every sport or setting, and the evidence covers intensities of about 6.9-9.3 RM.
paper.athleteDev: Strength training can be built into pre-season or in-season injury prevention plans, with weekly volume and intensity planned within the range studied. The review supports it as a prevention tool; it does not show a direct performance benefit.
paper.rtp: This review covers injury prevention in injury-free athletes, not rehabilitation after injury, so it cannot guide return-to-sport loading or readiness after an injury.

records.sourceFile: Systematic review of motion capture in virtual reality - Enhancing the precision of sports training.pdf

paper.citation: Li X, Fan D, Feng J, Lei Y, Cheng C, Li X. Systematic review of motion capture in virtual reality: enhancing the precision of sports training. Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments 2025;17(1):5-27.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examines the use of motion capture within virtual reality for sports training, covering 54 studies published 2018-2023. The authors describe applications in physical conditioning, cognitive training, sport-specific training, team collaboration and rehabilitation, and identify real-time feedback as the main benefit alongside hardware, data processing and interface limitations.
paper.tldr: This review of 54 studies describes how motion capture combined with virtual reality is being used in sports training, mainly to give real-time feedback. Many of the examples are small pilot or user studies, so the review maps possibilities rather than proving performance gains.
paper.methods: Literature review following PRISMA guidance across Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Embase and PubMed, limited to English articles published 2018-2023. Of 987 records, 756 remained after duplicate and title screening, 214 full texts were assessed, and 54 were included. Studies were summarized qualitatively by application theme and in tables of design, participants, VR setup and outcome measures.
paper.findings: The authors report that motion capture in VR offers real-time feedback, immersive training and tailored regimes across the reviewed applications. Examples include a basketball shooting algorithm that the authors say raised shooting percentages by up to 14% when combined with resistance training, and a randomized trial in which Kinect-based VR plus physical therapy improved upper extremity motor function in chronic stroke compared with physical therapy alone.
paper.limitations: The review reports no pooled effects and no per-study risk of bias ratings, although it describes using the Cochrane tool, and the synthesis is narrative. Many included studies are small pilot studies, and the authors' claims about AI, mixed reality and societal implications are forward-looking rather than drawn from the included studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Motion capture in VR may be worth piloting for technique feedback and decision-making practice, especially where real-time feedback is hard to give in the field. Before adoption, staff should check cybersickness, sensor comfort and whether skills transfer to the real sport, because the review does not establish transfer.
paper.athleteDev: Use VR with motion capture as a supplementary way to practise technique and decision-making, and check transfer with field performance measures before relying on it. The evidence base is mostly small pilot work, so it supports trialling the approach rather than adopting it as a performance standard.
paper.rtp: The review includes rehabilitation studies in stroke, neck pain and pediatric brain injury, but no return-to-sport criteria for athletes. It cannot be used to decide when an injured athlete is ready to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Talent Identification in Sport- A     Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Johnston K, Wattie N, Schorer J, Baker J. Talent identification in sport: a systematic review. Sports Med 2017.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 20 longitudinal and retrospective studies from 1990 to 2015 compared performance variables between highly skilled and less-skilled elite athletes. The authors found a high degree of variability in which factors discriminated skill levels, with physical profiles, male samples and athletes aged 10-20 years overrepresented.
paper.tldr: Across 20 longitudinal or retrospective studies, no set of performance measures consistently predicted later success in elite sport. Coaches should treat talent selection based on current test results as uncertain.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of English-language, peer-reviewed longitudinal or retrospective studies from January 1990 to July 2015, drawn from Web of Science and SPORTDiscus, reference lists and an expert panel. Studies had to compare at least two skill groups of elite or expert athletes over at least 12 months. Of 1695 unique records, 399 went to full-text review and 20 were included.
paper.findings: Sixteen studies were longitudinal, two retrospective and two mixed; 60% examined physical profiles, 65% included only males, and 60% examined athletes aged 10-20. Sprint ability discriminated skill levels in eight studies, agility drills did so in several sports, and none of the body composition measures distinguished skill levels. Results were inconsistent overall, and the authors report that all four mixed-measurement studies (physical, psychological and sport-specific variables) found some predictive utility.
paper.limitations: Only 20 studies met the criteria, and the review excluded grey-area topics such as relative age, birthplace and deliberate practice. Skill-level labels (elite, professional, selected, drafted) varied so much that comparisons are difficult, and only English peer-reviewed articles were included.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not rely on a single physical test or an early selection result for talent decisions; use several measures and track athletes over time. The authors argue that selecting athletes before age 10 lacks support, and that evidence for female athletes is especially thin.
paper.athleteDev: For talent decisions, combine physical, psychological and sport-specific measures and review athletes repeatedly rather than treating one test as predictive. The evidence base is thin for female athletes and for children under 10.
paper.rtp: This review covers talent selection in youth and elite athletes, not injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.
